citation.title: Rolling Memory: A New Approach to Annotation with Generative LLMs in Social and Political Research

question: Why do memory-based prompting approaches improve LLM text annotation, and can a two-run refinement (keeping 100 informative annotations from a first run in memory at the start of a second run) improve performance further over the standard memory approach and few-shot chain-of-thought?
data: Political nostalgia data from Müller and Proksch (2024): 1,200 human-annotated sentences from party manifestos in 24 European countries (151 nostalgic, 1,049 not). A subsample of 600 was used (all 151 nostalgic plus 449 random non-nostalgic). Model: GPT-4o via the OpenAI Python library, temperature 0.7. 20 reshuffled runs per approach. Human labels used as ground truth for validation only.
method: Compared zero-shot, few-shot with chain-of-thought (ten examples with reasoning), standard memory (each classification appended to the conversation history), and two-run memory (last 100 or peak 100 annotations from run 1 kept as initial memory for run 2, with a rolling window that drops the oldest entry). Performance measured as running F1 over rolling blocks of 200 observations, averaged over 20 reshuffled runs; t-tests and Cohen's d reported. Control: two consecutive few-shot CoT runs to test for leakage between runs.

definitions.definition: Information retained in the prompt, i.e. the model's own previous classifications kept in the conversation history.
definitions.quote: ‘Memory’, in this case, refers to the information retained in the prompt.

definitions.definition: LLMs updating their behaviour through examples in the prompt, without parameter (weight) updates.
definitions.quote: LLMs can update their behavior through examples in the prompt, without parameter updates

definitions.definition: Two-run variant: the last 100 classified observations from run 1 are used as the initial memory for run 2; run 2 classification is final.
definitions.quote: we take the last 100 classified observations in memory from run 1 and use them as the initial memory for run 2.

definitions.definition: Two-run variant: the set of 100 observations from run 1 that reached peak (highest average F1) performance is used as the initial memory for run 2.
definitions.quote: we calculate the set of 100 observations from run 1 that reached peak performance and use that set as the initial memory for run 2.

definitions.definition: Harmonic mean of precision and recall; preferred over accuracy for unbalanced samples.
definitions.quote: F1 is the harmonic mean between precision and recall and is a better metric than accuracy in unbalanced samples.

definitions.term: nostalgia (as coded in the validation data, quoting Müller and Proksch 2024)
definitions.definition: Predominately positive emotion associated with recalling memories of important or momentous events; a sentence is nostalgic when at least three of four coders agreed.
definitions.quote: A sentence is classified as nostalgic when at least three of the four coders agreed.

definitions.term: reinforcement memory (from Timoneda and Vallejo Vera 2025b)
definitions.definition: Memory approach where the model is also told whether its past labels were correct; needs hand-labelled data.
definitions.quote: letting the LLM if it correctly or incorrectly labeled the text, in addition to maintaining the annotated text in the prompt. They call this ‘reinforcement memory’.

proxies.indicator: Running F1 score for the nostalgic category against human-annotated ground truth, in rolling windows of 200 observations, averaged over 20 reshuffled runs.
proxies.quote: we report the average F1 scores across a rolling set of 200 observations.

proxies.indicator: Human inter-coder agreement: Cohen-type kappa for categorical judgments and ICC(2,k) for aggregated ratings.
proxies.quote: Coders showed moderate agreement on categorical judg­ ments (K = 0.56), while the aggregated ratings demonstrated good overall reliability (ICC(2,k) = 0.84, 95% CI [0.82, 0.85

proxies.concept: Whether gains come from text order or text difficulty rather than memory
proxies.indicator: Reshuffling the dataset 20 times and averaging running F1 across runs.
proxies.quote: By reshuffling the dataset ... 20 times and calculating the running average F1-scores for all the runs, we ensure it is not text complexity that is driving the results.

proxies.indicator: Two consecutive few-shot CoT runs without session restart; identical trajectories taken to show no carry-over.
proxies.quote: The two lines follow practically identical trajectories, which means that the first run does not in itself influence the results of a second run.

findings.claim: Zero-shot performance was low and flat (average F1 0.51); few-shot CoT raised average F1 to 0.694 with no trend over the run.
findings.quote: The average F1score for the zero-shot approach is low, at 0.51

findings.claim: Standard memory improved overall performance by about 9% on average over few-shot CoT, with diminishing returns and a plateau after about 400 observations; it was below few-shot CoT for roughly the first 250 observations.
findings.quote: the memory approach improves overall performance by 9%, on aver­ age after reshuffling the data 20 times

findings.claim: The two-run approach raised performance a further 3.56% (last 100) and 2.77% (peak 100), and 13.26% and 12.39% over few-shot CoT.
findings.quote: performance increases a further 3.56% using last 100 and ... 2.77% using peak 100.

findings.claim: Last 100 was marginally better than peak 100 (mean F1 0.786 vs 0.780); the difference was statistically significant but substantively small (Cohen's d 0.56).
findings.quote: The average F1-scores for the last-100 and peak-100 approaches are 0.786 and 0.780, respectively.

findings.claim: A second run of few-shot CoT without memory did not improve results, so gains in the two-run memory approach are attributed to the retained informative memory, not to repetition.
findings.quote: Figure 4 confirms this by showing that a second run does not improve the results for few-shot learning with CoT (no memory).

findings.claim: Performance converges towards the end of runs, which the authors read as a ceiling for generative LLMs in annotation.
findings.quote: performance converges towards the end of the run, pointing to the structural ceilings in terms of performance when using generative LLMs in annotation tasks.

findings.claim: LLM output varies across runs, so a single run may be high or low in the distribution of results.
findings.quote: researchers do not know whether the results they obtain from one run of their data are high or low in this distribution.

recommendations.claim: Use the last-100 two-run approach in practice rather than peak 100.
recommendations.quote: We therefore recommend using the last-100 approach in practice.

recommendations.claim: Where resources allow, reshuffle the data and run the annotation at least 10 times (akin to k-fold cross-validation), then take the run closest to the mean or adjudicate mismatches as with human annotators.
recommendations.quote: research­ ers are advised to reshuffle the dataset and run the process at least 10 times, which is akin to performing k-fold cross-validation.

recommendations.claim: Researchers should adopt multi-run evaluation strategies when computational resources allow.
recommendations.quote: When computational resources allow, we encourage researchers to adopt similar multi-run evaluation strategies.

recommendations.claim: Keep hand-labelled data for validation rather than for feeding the model, since the last-100 method does not need labelled examples.
recommendations.quote: allowing researcher to reduce the need for hand-labeled data (and use it, rather, for validation).

limitations.point: Proof of concept on one task (binary political nostalgia in translated manifesto sentences) and one model (GPT-4o); generalisation to more complex tasks, more labels, low-resource languages and rare categories is untested.
limitations.quote: in this article we provide a proof of concept for our rolling memory approach on one task.

limitations.point: The memory size of 100 is arbitrary; effects of other sizes on cost, overfitting and context limits are unknown.
limitations.quote: we use 100 observations to keep in memory, which is an arbitrary number derived from resource and token limit considerations.

limitations.point: Variance across runs is not formally modelled.
limitations.quote: formal modeling of the variance would provide additional nuance, such analysis is beyond the present scope

limitations.point: The dataset is unbalanced (151 vs 449 in the subsample), which makes the minority category harder for LLMs; human agreement on the task is only moderate (kappa 0.56), so ground-truth noise limits the F1 ceiling.
limitations.quote: The dataset is unbalanced, which is not a problem per se but does make it more difficult for LLMs to classify the underrepresented category correctly.

limitations.point: Non-English sentences were machine-translated to English before classification; the authors did not modify the text.
limitations.quote: the authors translated each non-English sentence into English before classification.

limitations.point: Results are probabilistic and depend on data order, so a single run is unreliable.
limitations.quote: LLM outputs are probabilistic and the dataset is reshuffled each time.

limitations.point: Prompt wording sensitivity was not tested; whether memory reduces the effect of prompt wording is left as future work.
limitations.quote: the degree to which memory approaches can reduce the effect of the wording in the prompt

limitations.point: Topic mismatch: the paper does not address organisation classification, business or fossil fuel linkage, or UNFCCC delegations; it supports only the method side (LLM annotation, validation against human labels, reproducibility). No injected instructions were found in the text.
